steps.title: Import React and Component from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and Component from the 'react' package. This will give you access to the core React library and the Component class for creating class components.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to import both React and Component from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and Component
import React, { Component } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and Component from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement should be added at the top of the file, making React and Component available for use.
successCriteria: The code must include a valid import statement that imports both React and Component from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and Component. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the Component class, which you'll need for creating class-based Error Boundaries.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import isn't quite complete. Make sure you're importing both React and Component from the 'react' package using the correct syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and Component from the 'react' package to proceed.

steps.title: Create the ErrorBoundary class component
steps.instruction: Create a class component named ErrorBoundary that extends React.Component. Define it after the import statement.
steps.hint: Use the class syntax with extends React.Component. You can leave the render method empty for now.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { Component } from 'react';

// Create the ErrorBoundary class component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A class component named ErrorBoundary is defined, extending React.Component.
successCriteria: The code should define a class named ErrorBoundary that extends React.Component and has a render method (can return null).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the ErrorBoundary class component. This is the foundation for implementing error boundaries in React.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your component is named exactly 'ErrorBoundary' and extends React.Component. Check your class syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Remember to use 'class ErrorBoundary extends React.Component' with a render method.

steps.title: Define the ErrorBoundaryProps interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named ErrorBoundaryProps with a single property: children of type React.ReactNode.
steps.hint: Create an interface using the 'interface' keyword, specifying the children prop type.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an ErrorBoundaryProps interface that defines the children prop type for your ErrorBoundary component.
successCriteria: The interface should be named ErrorBoundaryProps and include a children property typed as React.ReactNode.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've correctly defined the ErrorBoundaryProps interface with the children prop. This will provide type safety for the ErrorBoundary component's props.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your interface is named exactly 'ErrorBoundaryProps' and includes a 'children' property of type 'React.ReactNode'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Make sure to create an interface named ErrorBoundaryProps with a children property of type React.ReactNode.

steps.title: Define the ErrorBoundaryState interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named ErrorBoundaryState with a single property 'hasError' of type boolean.
steps.hint: Create an interface with the correct name and property type. Remember to export it if you want to use it elsewhere.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an ErrorBoundaryState interface with a boolean hasError property that will be used to track error state in the component.
successCriteria: interface ErrorBoundaryState
hasError: boolean
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the ErrorBoundaryState interface with the correct boolean property. This interface will be used to type the component's state in the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined an interface named ErrorBoundaryState with a hasError property of type boolean.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition doesn't match what's needed. Remember to create an interface named ErrorBoundaryState with a boolean hasError property.

steps.title: Apply interfaces to ErrorBoundary component
steps.instruction: Add the ErrorBoundaryState interface as the second generic type parameter to the ErrorBoundary class component.
steps.hint: The Component class from React accepts two generic type parameters: Props and State. You've already defined both interfaces in previous steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component should now have both ErrorBoundaryProps and ErrorBoundaryState as generic type parameters.
successCriteria: The ErrorBoundary class should extend Component with two generic type arguments: ErrorBoundaryProps and ErrorBoundaryState.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've correctly added both ErrorBoundaryProps and ErrorBoundaryState as generic type parameters to the ErrorBoundary component. This ensures TypeScript knows about both the props and state types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're adding ErrorBoundaryState as the second generic type parameter to the Component class. The syntax should be: `extends Component<ErrorBoundaryProps, ErrorBoundaryState>`.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ErrorBoundary component still needs the ErrorBoundaryState interface as a generic type parameter. Remember that React's Component class accepts two generic type parameters: Props and State.

steps.title: Initialize ErrorBoundary state
steps.instruction: Initialize the state in the ErrorBoundary constructor. Set the initial state with hasError as false and error as null.
steps.hint: Add a constructor method inside the ErrorBoundary class. Use super(props) and set this.state to match the ErrorBoundaryState interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a constructor that sets the initial state with hasError: false and error: null.
successCriteria: The constructor method is added to the ErrorBoundary class, calls super(props), and sets this.state to an object matching ErrorBoundaryState with hasError as false and error as null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the ErrorBoundary state. The constructor properly sets the initial state with hasError: false and error: null, which matches the ErrorBoundaryState interface.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are some issues. Make sure you have a constructor method that calls super(props) and sets this.state to an object with both hasError and error properties. hasError should be false and error should be null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization is missing or incorrect. You need to add a constructor method to the ErrorBoundary class that calls super(props) and sets this.state to { hasError: false, error: null }.

steps.title: Implement getDerivedStateFromError lifecycle method
steps.instruction: Add the static getDerivedStateFromError lifecycle method to your ErrorBoundary class. This method should receive an error parameter and return an object that updates the state to indicate an error has occurred.
steps.hint: Inside the ErrorBoundary class, add a static method named getDerivedStateFromError that takes an error parameter and returns { hasError: true, error: error }.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary class now has a static getDerivedStateFromError method that will be called when an error occurs in any child component, allowing the boundary to update its state accordingly.
successCriteria: Method is static
Method name is getDerivedStateFromError
Method takes an error parameter
Method returns an object with hasError: true
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the getDerivedStateFromError lifecycle method. This static method will be automatically called by React when an error occurs in any child component, allowing your ErrorBoundary to update its state to reflect the error.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are some issues. Make sure the method is static, takes an error parameter, and returns an object with hasError: true. Also ensure the method name is exactly getDerivedStateFromError.
steps.feedbackWrong: The getDerivedStateFromError method is not implemented correctly. Remember that this should be a static method inside the ErrorBoundary class that takes an error parameter and returns an object to update the state.

steps.title: Implement componentDidCatch lifecycle method
steps.instruction: Inside the ErrorBoundary class component, add the componentDidCatch lifecycle method that logs the error and errorInfo to the console.
steps.hint: The componentDidCatch method receives two parameters: error and errorInfo. Use console.error to log them.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a componentDidCatch method that logs error details to the console when an error occurs in its child components.
successCriteria: The componentDidCatch method is defined inside the ErrorBoundary class
It has two parameters: error (type Error) and errorInfo (type React.ErrorInfo)
It logs the error and errorInfo using console.error
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the componentDidCatch lifecycle method. This method will be called when an error occurs in any child component, allowing you to log error details for debugging.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your componentDidCatch method correctly logs both the error and errorInfo parameters. Make sure you're using console.error to log them.
steps.feedbackWrong: The componentDidCatch method is missing or incorrect. Remember to add this lifecycle method inside the ErrorBoundary class with two parameters (error and errorInfo) and log them using console.error.

steps.title: Add render method structure
steps.instruction: Add a render method to the ErrorBoundary class component. The method should return JSX with conditional rendering: if hasError is true, show an error message; otherwise, render the children.
steps.hint: In class components, the render method is required. Use this.state.hasError to check the error state, and this.props.children to access the children prop.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now has a render method that conditionally renders an error message or the children based on the hasError state.
successCriteria: render method defined
conditional logic using this.state.hasError
returns JSX with error message when hasError is true
returns this.props.children when hasError is false
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the render method with conditional rendering. The ErrorBoundary can now display different content based on whether an error has occurred.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the render method needs both conditional branches. Make sure to check this.state.hasError and return appropriate JSX for both true and false cases.
steps.feedbackWrong: The render method is missing or incomplete. Remember to add a render method that returns JSX and uses this.state.hasError to decide what to show.

steps.title: Implement error state UI
steps.instruction: In the render method, add conditional rendering to return error message UI when hasError is true. Use the existing state variables to display the error.
steps.hint: Check if this.state.hasError is true, then return JSX showing an error message with this.state.error details.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component now displays a user-friendly error message when an error occurs in its children.
successCriteria: Conditional check for this.state.hasError
Return JSX with error message
Use this.state.error in the UI
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the error state UI. The ErrorBoundary will now show a helpful message when an error occurs.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking this.state.hasError and returning appropriate JSX when it's true. Also include the error details from this.state.error.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error state UI isn't implemented correctly. You need to add conditional rendering in the render method to check if this.state.hasError is true and return error message JSX.

steps.title: Implement normal state UI
steps.instruction: In the render method, add a conditional check to return this.props.children when hasError is false.
steps.hint: Use an if statement or ternary operator to check this.state.hasError. When it's false, return this.props.children.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component will now properly render children when no error has occurred.
successCriteria: Conditional check for this.state.hasError
Return this.props.children when hasError is false
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the normal state UI. The ErrorBoundary will now render children when no errors are present.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to check this.state.hasError and return this.props.children when it's false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The render method should check this.state.hasError and return this.props.children when no error is present.

steps.title: Export the ErrorBoundary component
steps.instruction: Export the ErrorBoundary component as the default export so it can be imported in other files.
steps.hint: Use the 'export default' syntax followed by the component name.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ErrorBoundary component is exported as default, making it available for import in other files.
successCriteria: The code includes 'export default ErrorBoundary;' at the end of the file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully exported the ErrorBoundary component as default. This makes it ready to be imported and used in other parts of your application.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using 'export default ErrorBoundary;' exactly as shown. Check that the component name matches exactly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ErrorBoundary component needs to be exported as default. Add 'export default ErrorBoundary;' at the end of the file.
